The Talents
TAL-ents
noun phrase
From the Greek talanton, a great weight or sum of money, the trust committed to the servants in the Lord’s parable of stewardship.

Biblical Definition

The parable of the talents teaches that the Lord Jesus Christ, going away into a far country, commits to His servants a trust to be used for His glory until He returns, and will reckon with each according to his faithfulness. He delivered unto them his goods; unto one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to every man according to his several ability (Mat 25:15). The first two traded with their talents and gained as much again; but he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord’s money (Mat 25:18). After a long time the lord returned and reckoned with them. To the faithful He said, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord (Mat 25:21). But the slothful servant, who had hidden his talent and charged his lord with hardness, was condemned as wicked and unprofitable, and cast into outer darkness. The dictionary marks this parable as the rule of Christian stewardship: every gift, office, and opportunity is a trust from the Lord, to be improved for Him. The faithful servant is not saved by his works but shows by them the grace that wrought in him; the slothful servant, hiding his trust, betrays a heart that never knew its Master. So the faithful enter into the joy of their Lord.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Lord’s parable of servants entrusted with talents, teaching faithful stewardship and the reckoning at His return.

expand to see more

THE TALENTS, the Lord’s parable of servants entrusted with His goods.

To each he gave according to his several ability, five, two, and one.

Two traded and gained; one hid his talent in the earth.

The faithful heard, Well done, thou good and faithful servant.

The slothful was cast as unprofitable into outer darkness.

Key Scripture

Mat 25:15 — "And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey."

Mat 25:18 — "But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord’s money."

Mat 25:21 — "His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."

Mat 25:29 — "For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath."

Modern Corruption

A parable of Scripture; it teaches that every gift is a trust from the Lord, to be improved for Him against the day of reckoning.

expand to see more

The talents have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s great parable of stewardship. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the reckoning that awaits every servant for the trust committed to him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every gift, office, and opportunity is a trust from the Lord, to be improved for His glory until He comes. The faithful servants traded and gained, and entered into the joy of their lord; the slothful hid his trust and was cast out, his unfaithfulness betraying a heart that never truly knew its Master. So the parable teaches that good works do not earn salvation but flow from the grace that wrought within, and that the day of reckoning will divide the faithful from the false. Let every soul use what God has given, that it may hear, Well done, thou good and faithful servant.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for a weight of money, the parable names the trust committed to the servants of Christ.

expand to see more

The Talents — from the Greek talanton, a great weight or sum of money.

The lord delivered his goods to his servants before his journey.

Each received according to his several ability.

Two traded and gained; one hid his talent.

The faithful entered the joy of their lord; the slothful was cast out.

Usage

"Like the faithful servants, the saint trades with the trust his Lord has given."

"Well done, thou good and faithful servant: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."

"Every gift is a stewardship, and the slothful who hides his trust is cast out."
